title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
claim: Existing methods each sacrifice one of accuracy, interpretability, or abstention, and shape-based concept spaces conflate regimes that prediction-grounded concept spaces separate.
layout: 2 panels: left triangle of goals, right shape-space vs predictive-space with central segments
description: The figure has two rounded panels. The left panel is a triangle with Accuracy at the top, Interpretability at the bottom left and Calibrated Abstention at the bottom right. Colored circles on the edges and corners mark method families such as black-box models, post-hoc explainers, time-series concept bottleneck models (CBMs), adaptive segmentation, selective prediction and conceptual safeguards. Each family sits near the goal it emphasizes. A large gold star labeled ConceptTime sits at the center, so the eye goes there first. The right panel has three parts. On the left is a 2-D scatter of shape-guided dimensions where points A and B sit close together and C and D sit apart. In the middle is a dashed box of four time-series segments, A to D, each shown with a faded context and a bold highlighted segment. On the right is a plot of predictive variance against negative log likelihood. A, C and D form clusters and B is isolated in its own cloud. Colors link the segments to the points.
caption: ConceptTime targets accuracy, interpretability, and calibrated abstention through a single self-supervised primitive. Left, existing methods emphasize different goals. Right, 4 segments (A-D) and their preceding context. Raw-shape space conflates A and B (both end calm) and splits C from D. Predictive-geometry space, spanned by predictive variance and NLL, collapses A, C, and D as expectation is satisfied and isolates B as a surprise. Concepts grounded in deviation from prediction, therefore, distinguish dynamical regimes that shape-based vocabularies cannot.
abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.
